title: Modi Faces Diplomatic Marathon With SCO, BRICS, and UNGA Summits in Six-Week Sprint
excerpt: From Bishkek to New Delhi to New York, the Indian PM will navigate a packed global calendar that tests India's balancing act between rival power blocs.
body:
• PM Modi is set to attend the SCO summit in Bishkek, host the BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 12–13, and address the UNGA on September 26 — three major multilateral engagements in roughly six weeks.
  • India will host the 18th BRICS Summit under its chairmanship theme "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability," with Russian President Vladimir Putin expected to attend on Modi's personal invitation.
  • At UNGA, Modi will deliver India's address during the 80th-anniversary session alongside leaders including Donald Trump, Netanyahu, and Shehbaz Sharif.
  • The tight calendar underscores India's growing diplomatic ambitions as it navigates complex ties with both Western allies and the Russia-China axis.

Three Summits, Six Weeks

Prime Minister Narendra Modi is heading into the most concentrated stretch of multilateral diplomacy of his tenure. Beginning with the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek this August, followed by India's hosting of the BRICS leaders' summit in New Delhi on September 12–13, and capped by his address to the UN General Assembly in New York on September 26, Modi will engage with nearly every major power bloc on the global stage in a matter of weeks.

https://x.com/CNNnews18/status/2081611988334162146

The schedule — three high-stakes summits in roughly six weeks — is unprecedented for an Indian leader in a single diplomatic season. It places India simultaneously at the table of the China- and Russia-anchored SCO, the expanded 11-member BRICS grouping, and the UN's premier global assembly, testing New Delhi's ability to maintain its strategic autonomy across increasingly polarised forums.

BRICS: India Takes Center Stage

The BRICS summit represents the marquee event. India assumed the grouping's rotating chairmanship on January 1 and has spent the year building toward the New Delhi gathering under the theme "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability." The foreign ministers of BRICS member nations already convened in the capital in May to lay the groundwork.

The 18th summit will bring together leaders from 11 full members — Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, and the UAE — along with 10 partner nations. Russia's Deputy Foreign Ministry has confirmed that President Vladimir Putin is likely to travel to New Delhi on Modi's personal invitation, a visit that would carry significant geopolitical weight amid sustained Western pressure over the Ukraine conflict.

"India will attempt to give a new form to BRICS... in the spirit of people-centricity and humanity first."

— Prime Minister Narendra Modi, at the 2025 Rio Summit

India has also extended a rare invitation to Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman as a special guest, signalling New Delhi's intent to use its chairmanship to strengthen regional ties. The summit agenda is expected to focus on trade, technology, climate finance, reform of global institutions, and supply-chain resilience — priorities that align with India's broader pitch as a bridge between advanced economies and the developing world.

UNGA: The UN's 80th Anniversary

Two weeks after the BRICS summit wraps up, Modi is scheduled to fly to New York for the 80th session of the UN General Assembly. According to the preliminary speakers' list, India's head of government will address the high-level General Debate on the morning of September 26 — preceded by the leaders of Israel, China, and the UK, and followed by Pakistan's Shehbaz Sharif.

The session carries additional symbolic weight as the UN marks its 80th anniversary under the theme "Better Together: 80 Years and More for Peace, Development and Human Rights." A commemorative high-level meeting is set for September 22, with the regular debate running from September 23 to 29. US President Donald Trump will deliver his first UNGA address since returning to office on the opening day.

For Modi, the address will be his seventh to the General Assembly's high-level session. India's push for UN Security Council reform and a permanent seat — a long-standing demand backed by several BRICS members — is expected to feature prominently in his remarks.

SCO: Anti-Terror Agenda in Bishkek

The diplomatic season opens with the SCO leaders' summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. The SCO foreign ministers met in the Kyrgyz capital last week to finalise the agenda, with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi holding bilateral meetings with counterparts from Belarus and Uzbekistan on the summit's sidelines.

India has been pressing the 10-member grouping for a stronger stance on cross-border terrorism, a position that has sometimes put New Delhi at odds with fellow members Pakistan and China. At the most recent SCO summit in Tianjin last year, India refused to sign a joint statement that failed to mention the Pahalgam terror attack — a calculated move that underscored New Delhi's willingness to break with bloc consensus on issues it considers non-negotiable.

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh already represented India at the SCO Defence Ministers' Meeting in Bishkek in April, where discussions focused on counter-terrorism coordination and regional stability.

The Balancing Act

The compressed calendar highlights a central tension in India's foreign policy: maintaining warm ties with Russia and China through forums like the SCO and BRICS while deepening strategic partnerships with the United States, Japan, and Australia through the Quad and bilateral channels.

India recently sealed a new Defence Framework with the US on the sidelines of the ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting, reaffirmed its Quad commitment at the Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Manila, and declared 2026 the "ASEAN-India Year of Maritime Cooperation." At the same time, Modi personally invited Xi Jinping to the BRICS summit during their bilateral at the Tianjin SCO meeting last year, and Russia remains one of India's largest energy and defence suppliers.

For the Indian diaspora, the diplomatic marathon carries direct implications. Immigration policy, trade agreements, and geopolitical stability all flow from the relationships Modi builds at these summits. How India navigates the space between competing power centres — and whether it can translate summit diplomacy into concrete outcomes on trade, technology, and institutional reform — will define New Delhi's global standing through the rest of the decade.
